tagline: A snail that flies like an insect
summary: The sea butterfly is a tiny swimming snail, its glassy shell often under a centimetre across, that 'flies' through Arctic and subarctic seas on two wing-like flaps. Hugely abundant and a key food for fish, whales and the sea angel, its fragile shell makes it an early warning sign of ocean acidification.

stats.size: Shell about 5–10 mm wide (up to about 13 mm)
stats.range: Arctic and subarctic seas of the Atlantic and Pacific
stats.diet: Phytoplankton, tiny protozoans and small zooplankton caught in a mucus web

facts.title: Flying, not swimming
facts.text: It beats two wing-like flaps 4 to 10 times a second in a stroke resembling that of tiny flying insects, effectively flying through the water.

facts.title: A net made of mucus
facts.text: It hangs still beneath a large, spherical web of mucus that traps plankton, then eats the web and its catch and spins a new one.

facts.title: A shell that dissolves
facts.text: Its thin shell is made of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate that dissolves easily. In experiments, shell damage increased steadily as seawater became more acidic.

facts.title: Arctic food staple
facts.text: It can make up more than half of all zooplankton in polar waters and is eaten by herring, salmon, seals, whales, seabirds and sea angels.

facts.title: Male first, then female
facts.text: Each sea butterfly starts life as a male and later becomes female once it grows larger than about 5 mm.

references.title: Shell condition and survival of Puget Sound pteropods are impaired by ocean acidification conditions (Busch et al. 2014, PLoS ONE)

image.alt: A tiny sea butterfly against a dark, speckled background: a glassy coiled shell with pinkish-brown insides and two translucent wing-like flaps spread above it, with a red 1000 micrometre scale bar in the corner
image.caption: Sea butterfly from the Arctic, photographed during NOAA's Hidden Ocean expedition (2005)
image.creator: Russ Hopcroft, Institute of Marine Science, University of Alaska Fairbanks / NOAA

notes: IMAGE IS LOW-RESOLUTION (600×450, not upscaled; encoded at q100 to pass 30 KB check) and has a small scale bar in the bottom-left corner. It is the only correctly identified live L. helicina photo on Commons; all ≥1200 px files were multi-species figures, a museum label sheet, or the NOAA 'dissolved pteropod shell' image (species not stated). Editor may prefer image: null or a licensed replacement. Antarctic animals formerly called L. helicina are now L. antarctica (Wikipedia, citing Hunt et al. 2010). Flight, mucus-web, abundance, predator and sex-change facts are from Wikipedia (secondary; cites Murphy et al., Gilmer & Harbison 1991, Hunt et al. 2010). Category "transparent" is borderline: the shell is described as hyaline (glass-clear) and the wings translucent, but the body is dark purple.
